title: Payment System (Stripe)
summary: Move money exactly once: idempotent payment intents, a state machine around an external payment processor, a double-entry ledger, webhooks, and daily reconciliation.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Merchants create payments, customers pay by card; refunds
Notify merchants of outcomes (webhooks); merchant balances and payouts
Never charge twice; never lose a payment (correctness over latency)
Auditable: every balance derivable from immutable entries
PCI scope minimised — raw card numbers in as few systems as possible

blocks.text: Volume is modest; the difficulty is correctness across unreliable networks and external systems.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Idempotency keys are stored with the request hash and the response. A retry with the same key returns the stored response — even if the first attempt is still running (return 409 / in-progress).

sections.title: Deep dive: state machine and exactly-once effects

items.title: Create
items.text: Insert the intent with status `requires_confirmation` and the idempotency key (unique constraint).

items.title: Confirm
items.text: Move to `processing` and persist the outgoing processor request id *before* calling the processor.

items.title: Call processor
items.text: Send the request with our own idempotency key; processors dedupe on it.

items.title: Unknown outcome
items.text: On timeout, do not retry blindly — query the processor by our request id, or let reconciliation settle it.

items.title: Record
items.text: On success write ledger entries and status `succeeded` in one transaction, plus an outbox event.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Treating a timeout as a failure and letting the customer retry. The first attempt may have succeeded — that's how double charges happen.

items: Every transaction's debits equal its credits; balances are sums over entries — never mutable counters as the source of truth.
Entries are immutable; corrections are new reversing entries.
Store amounts as integers in minor units (cents) with a currency code — never floats.
Webhooks: at-least-once delivery from the outbox with exponential backoff for days; merchants must dedupe on event id; sign payloads (HMAC).
Reconciliation: each day, match processor settlement files against the ledger; mismatches go to an exceptions queue (auto-fix where rules allow, otherwise humans).
Reconciliation is what catches every case the online path got wrong — design for it, don't bolt it on.
Shard intents and ledger by merchant/account; keep a transaction's entries on one shard.
Processor outages: route to a secondary processor where possible; queue confirmations.
Hot merchant accounts: batch ledger writes or use sub-accounts summed periodically.
PCI: tokenise at the edge so only the vault sees PANs.

cols.title: Synchronous confirm
cons: Long-tail processor latency hits the merchant's request

cols.title: Async with webhooks
pros: Resilient to slow processors; handles 3-D Secure flows

items.title: Deep dives
items.text: State machine + unknown outcomes; double entry.

items.q: How long do you keep idempotency keys?
items.a: 24 hours is typical — long enough to cover client retries.

items.q: How do you handle currency conversion?
items.a: Record both legs with the FX rate used as separate ledger entries; never mutate.
A scheduled job sums available merchant balance, creates a payout transaction (ledger entries) and calls the bank via a payout rail.

items: Idempotency key on every mutating call — ours and the processor's.
Persist intent before calling out; query on timeout.
Daily reconciliation is part of the design.
